title: Everyone wants bigger context windows. Linus Lee thinks that's the wrong instinct

segments.text: So, so Linus, um,
before we get started, I just wanted to
ask you, like what's the motivation to
go into VC? You're ahead of AI
at Thrive now, and you come from a
product company.
>> Yeah,
I've gotten this question a few times. I
don't really think of it as
moving from product to VC. I think of it
as I've always operated from
trying to find and answer questions that
I'm personally interested in.
And the question that I've been obsessed
with for a long time people's
relationship to information. How people
retrieve information, understand
information, and make sense of it. Data
visualizations, interpreting data sets,
trying to figure out new and interesting
questions to ask. In some ways, I spent
time at Ocean trying to do this both in
the product and then also in how we try
to understand how people use the
product.
Um, and when I came to Thrive, I was I
was still interested in this, in
particular, looking at it through the
lens of model interpretability.
Um,
one way to look at models is as a way as
a function that takes inputs and
generates outputs, but another way to
look at it as as as kind of a lens into
the training data set of models. And so,
by
applying models or training models on
interesting data sets and then studying
them, it's an interesting way to try to
study trends in data sets that the
models are trained on. And so, I was
thinking about these questions and
getting more and more interested in
how models can help us understand more
and more complex data sets. And an
interesting place where there's a lot of
impact and value from understanding
complex semi-structured data is in
investing. And so, that combined with my
general love of working with people who
are building new and interesting
creative things in the world in the
world of AI kind of led me here, but a
lot of the work that I do today, I still
think of as fundamentally about helping
people
understand and make sense of more and
more interesting kinds of data and data
sets.
>> That's great. And what what is it that
you found most interesting in terms of
the the types of data sets that you have
a chance to work with now that you might
not have explored before?
>> I think there are a couple of different
uh
maybe lessons that I've learned or ideas
that I've I've encountered. One that I
learned fairly quickly coming from
um a product like Notion to some of the
things that um I thought about more
recently is
the the distinction and the pros and
cons of unstructured versus structured
data.
Notion was very unstructured data pill
in some ways where you kind of imagine
everything that happens inside a company
or inside the product as you know,
everything is at the end of the day just
a bunch of text on pages and then you
try to build up a world a model of the
world from that. Um where in the real
world, it turns out there's a lot of
structured data already and a lot of
questions people want to answer are not
just looking for facts or looking for
knowledge or stories, but also
aggregating across time, aggregate
across different dimensions, looking at
a lot of quantitative data, um
trying to answer questions like how has
the importance of this category versus
that category shifted over time, what is
the frequency of these events versus
those events? And so, you know, in the
real world there's you kind of can never
get away from There's there's a level of
elegance that
I used to find in purely thinking of the
world as just a bunch of text. And um
I think one of the things I came to
realize is actually that is unrealistic
in many ways and if you want to answer
really important questions that people
actually care about, you have to
be able to shift
fluidly between working with structured
data and unstructured data. Um and I
think the way that language models can
be harnessed for
these two different worlds are slightly
different. So, that that's one kind of
dichotomy that I thought about a lot
recently. Um
Another interesting idea that's been on
my mind
uh uh, which I don't know if this will
make the cut or not, but I'll just kind
of talk about it, is
the role that
how you index the data plays in what you
can do with the data.
Um, this is something I also want to
talk about more in in my main talk, but
one of the cool things that you can do
once you have vertically integrated
control of not just what data that you
have to begin with, but how you how you
ingest that data is you can do a lot of
the like
massaging of the data to pre-structure
it when you're indexing it at indexing
time or at write time, and then that
allows you to make certain kinds of
queries that you would never be able to
make if all you had was just a
collection of pages or a or a record
index. Um, and so I I've analogized it
to many of my friends to trying to work
with satellite imagery or web indexes.
So, these very very very low-level data
sets where a lot of the work in trying
to make these data sets useful is
pre-structuring it, pre-parcelling out
these
interesting patterns or semantic units,
and then you can make more and more
interesting queries on top of it. And
so, how much of the work should you do
at write time versus read time is
another kind of big question that I've
been exploring.
>> And how do you think about that? Do you
work backwards from what you want the
output of the use case, um, or the
output of the query to be, and then
figure out sort of what the data needs
to look like, the optimal data structure
on on the ingest, or do you have a a
mental model for actually effecting this
in a system?
>> I think it's hard to answer these kinds
of questions decoupled from a particular
use case.
And and it also depends on the
technology that's available, right?
In in most specific use cases there's
there's already there's already
something that humans are doing. So,
you're oftentimes, if you go out in the
real world, people will be
already doing a lot of the work of
pre-structuring the data into a
spreadsheet, into a project tracker,
into a table in Microsoft Excel or
something. And so, you can already look
at kind of organic structures that have
emerged in the course of people doing
the work manually, and then start with
that as the as the base, and then think
about
the work that needs to happen as kind of
indexing into that structure and then
and then reading out of that structure.
And so that's that's one good place to
start.
I also one of the more kind of
academically interesting, conceptually
interesting threads related to this is
sometimes you can you can mess with the
representation that you use to store the
data. And so
I haven't spent too much time recently
thinking about this, but one of the
ideas that I was really really obsessed
with a couple of years ago was whether
you could use sparse vectors derived
from interpretability techniques as a
way to index data. So instead of just
dense vectors, which are just
you know, you you chop the head off the
model and then whatever is inside the
model as the data passes through the
model is the embedding. But instead of
just using those raw embeddings where
individual dimensions don't mean
anything, if you could apply mechanistic
interpretability techniques like sparse
autoencoders to get a sparse vector
where each dimension actually means
something legible to a human, maybe you
can use those sparse vectors where a a
dimension may mean a particular
sentiment, or dimension may mean the
presence of some idea, and you could
using a totally different representation
of a document or of an idea or of a
concept, you could index into that data
and make kinds of queries that you
otherwise couldn't make. And so I guess
this brings us back to my answer to the
previous question again, which is
in addition to thinking about how you
retrieve the data, there's a lot of
design space that's wide open in how you
index the data and store the data that
can totally open up new kinds of queries
that you can make over the data set
itself.
>> Yeah, totally agree.
Well, I want to acknowledge your um talk
coming up at AI Council, which sounds
awesome, context engineering on the
frontier. And I noticed that you comment
on how context windows are an expensive
and incomplete workaround in your
abstract. Um what is the trap that you
find most engineers fall into when they
embrace this method of speaking to the
model.
>> Everything is a trade-off, right? I
think
even internally oftentimes
the first prototype that you build, you
just try to throw everything into the
model context, and it's a good baseline,
but then you want to try to improve upon
it for latency reasons, for cost
reasons. Often I think an underrated
reason to do these kinds of design
experiments is also for engineering
flexibility reasons. What I mean by that
is if you have a single agent or a
single um inference doing that single
kind of monolithic you know, inference
stack doing the full task, and then you
want to change some part of it. If it's
a single agent, then changing any part
of it could technically influence how
the model performs in any other part of
it. And so if you change something about
the system prompt or change the
description of a particular tool, you
have to run all of the evals again of
anything that touches this particular
generation stack because it's one
monolithic system, where
I think one of the under-discussed
benefits of techniques like retrieval
sub-agents is that not only is it saving
costs and potentially saving latency and
improving performance, but it also
breaks the total system down into
composable sub-pieces, where you can
they they have better defined
interfaces, so you can iterate on just
the retrieval sub-agent and make it
really really good, and then that
doesn't impact the rest of how the
top-level agent interacts with all of
his other tools. So
that's that's a kind of an
under-discussed reason to try to build
bigger systems out of these more
composable units. And And I think that
that leads me to I think one of the
high-level ideas I want to talk about in
in in the talk, which is
retrieval isn't just
you know, I have a tool or I have a
collection of tools that cause into a
data set. It's also
what goes in in building the data set,
and then also all the different um
gradations of steps of how that how the
data end up in the final model's
context, you can use tools you can kind
of think of a sub agent as just a very
expensive tool. So, you could use a sub
agent which is a very expensive tool
call, you could also have a lighter
weight tool that does heavier
re-ranking, but it's not quite a
full agent. You could have a sub agent
that writes structured queries over over
structured data set or relational
database for example. And so,
um
I think the design space is less just
um what do we put in the context and how
long is the context and more okay, we
can spend the expensive tokens in the
final model's context and that has some
trade-offs, or we can push some of that
retrieval work down into
uh more and more specific tools that are
less and less and less costly, but
require maybe a little more design
thinking. And so, I think that that uh
kind of a roundabout way to answer, but
the the question on context is about
um
how do you trade off between
the benefits of putting everything in
one monolithic context versus spreading
that work out over smaller models or
more more dedicated tools to make sure
that at the end of the day your metrics,
which may be, you know, precision or
maybe the completeness of the answer or
maybe the speed like how do you, you
know, how do how do you fulfill the
final metrics that you want to do to
fulfill in performance uh using all of
these like the the full bag of
techniques that are available to you
from getting the information for the
data set into the final model's context.
>> Well, I've heard you say that um or
reframe context engineering as a search
problem. Um what exactly did you mean by
that? And is is that related?
>> Yeah, totally. Um one of the things that
I'm prone to doing is kind of take very
modern problems and then try to call out
uh how age-old computer science problems
relate to it. And um actually earlier
today I had this image which I'm
probably going to use in the talk
uh which is this comic from I think
Uh
uh there was I think made originally for
for IBM, which is about information
retrieval. And it's it's kind of funny
because it takes a very complex problem
and tries to boil it down into these
simple simple terms. But the comic
basically says, "Information retrieval
is all about like structuring the
information you have into terms that the
computers can understand." Where you
want to bring in just enough information
to answer the questions that the user
wants, but not so much that you
overwhelm the computer. And that's
really what all information retrieval
is. It's like at the end of the day,
it's like trading off between precision
and recall by trying to translate the
data into ways that the
computer can understand. And it's just
such a profound way to think about even
everything that agents are doing.
Um,
but uh, so information retrieval is like
one classic idea you can apply to think
about agents. And and then all of the
literature from the last 50, 60 years of
uh research into this domain you can
bring into the new world of agents.
>> Mhm.
>> Another classic idea is search, which is
to say you define some space of options
or space of documents that you are
trying to optimize some set of values
over. And then you have some way of like
either narrowing down your search space
or enumerating the space so that you can
you can iteratively search through it.
Um, and you can apply this I think in in
a bunch of different ways. I think one
of the one of the classic techniques
techniques have very high-level
techniques in search is just iterative
refinement, right? Like in a lot of
production search stacks, even unrelated
to language models, you will see you
start with a very large data set, you
have a very fast retriever-reranker that
that kind of over-retrieves, and then
you have stages of progressive
refinement and narrowing. Initially
you're optimizing for recall, and then
over time you're optimizing for
precision to get to the final result.
Um and
re- relating to what I said a moment ago
of it's not just what's in the tool,
it's actually all these different
techniques that you can apply. I think
an idea that I'm starting to use a lot
more in my work and I'm starting to see
elsewhere in the ecosystem is
uh
in the process of getting the data from
the originating data set into the final
kind of top-level agents models
contacts.
You can apply the same mindset of
iterative refinement where you over
retrieve initially and then you use
whether it's re-rankers or sub-agents or
maybe you run the multiple methods in
parallel and try to union them together
or try to merge their rankings. All
these different techniques you can you
can combine to have this kind of
iterative refinement pipeline pipeline
before the data makes it into the into
the final model and it's a one of the
many kind of classic ideas from search
and retrieval to think about
and contacts.
>> Very cool.
Well, before I let you go, I just wanted
to ask you one more thing. Um, you
mentioned that you've used
tens of billions of tokens at Thrive um,
in your work there so far.
Um, I'm just curious to to understand
more about like what what that what that
really means at the end of the day and
um, is there a failure mode uh, at that
scale that you feel like folks are not
talking about publicly yet?
>> That figure came from when I spoke about
some of what we built last year. Um, I
think now we are a bit we're we're quite
a bit beyond it both in magnitude but
also in terms of how we think about
measuring progress. A lot more of what
we think about these days is more about
adoption and results and so are people
using it? What are people doing with it?
Um,
but regardless of whether you're
measuring usage and outcomes or you
you're measuring inputs like tokens, I
think one
failure mode is as you get more scale,
it starts to become harder and harder to
actually know what's going on, how these
things are failing, whether they're
failing. Um, it's easy to end up
building these systems in a way where
you
uh,
don't even have a day-to-day sense of
how many how what percent of the runs
that you're running in production are
achieving successful outcomes as defined
by the user and so understanding
observability monitoring, I think gets
really difficult. Um, and observability,
I think I think a lot of folks in this
domain used to refer to the health of
the infrastructure and the software
system which is certainly one way to
think about it is like how many runs are
completing successfully at the
infrastructural level.
But I think an even more important one
that's even harder to stay on top of
just intuitively is are
are these runs or are these pipelines
delivering results in a way that is sort
of semantically successful in the way
that the user would define it. Like when
they want to generate a deck, is there a
deck at the end of it or is the model
kind of stumbling through and not, you
know, delivering a text answer instead?
And so um one one kind of
domain in this area that or or one kind
of work that I'm excited about in this
area is
can you build tools to help people as
you scale up
stay on top of and kind of get a
retain like a hand feel for how people
are using the tools that they're
building and
um
are the are are the models struggling?
What tools are models struggling with?
Like when you're when you're using
coding agents on your own laptop, uh
you know intuitively what tools are hard
and where models bump into problems, but
you just lose track of that when when
you're running this
at at higher scale. I think you can you
can build tools to help pull that
feeling back into your hands.
>> Re- recover that. Well, that's great,
Linus. Um yeah, very excited to hear
your talk uh context engineering at the
frontier and
thanks for chatting about it in in
advance of the conference and I look
forward to seeing you there.
>> Me as well. I'm very excited.
